demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Threat.value: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper

issues.item: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
issues.explanation: 'Threat in Delays' suggests a broad expectancy of external danger from uncertainty/delays, which fits poorly with the stated trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another; the rest of the profile centers on guilt, recall-based distress, and hypervigilance rather than delay-specific threat meanings.

issues.item: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body
issues.explanation: 'Body Unreliable' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile and trauma type. For a patient whose trauma was accidentally injuring another, the appraisals presented otherwise focus on guilt, inadequacy, and permanent moral/personal change. A loss of trust in one's body usually implies prominent bodily injury, dissociation, panic-like symptoms, or functional impairment, none of which are represented elsewhere in Triggers, Memory, Threat, or Strategies.

vignette:
Arthur was a man who had built his life on predictability. For forty years, he had worked as a bank teller, his days governed by opening hours, balanced ledgers, and the quiet hum of financial routine. At sixty-two, he looked forward to a retirement spent with his wife, Mary, and doting on his grandson, Leo. That sense of order shattered six months ago in his own garage. He had been on a stepladder, trying to secure a high shelf, when five-year-old Leo, who he thought was inside with Mary, darted in to show him a drawing. Startled, Arthur’s arm jerked, knocking a heavy metal toolbox from the top of the ladder. He remembers the sickening thud, a sound that now plays on a loop in his mind, followed by a silence that felt louder than a scream. The memory never comes as a full narrative, but rather as sudden, unwelcome pieces: the bright red of Leo’s shirt, the unnatural angle of his head, the feeling of his own hands shaking so violently he couldn’t dial 911 properly.

In the weeks that followed Leo’s recovery from a serious concussion and fractured clavicle, the fragments of that afternoon began to ambush Arthur. When he tried to recall the event, the same raw terror he felt in that moment would seize him, his heart hammering against his ribs as if he were back in the garage. This terror was always followed by a wave of profound guilt that left him breathless. The memories were so potent that they fueled a constant, exhausting state of vigilance. He found he could no longer relax, even sitting in his favourite armchair with the evening paper. Every creak of the floorboards, every car that passed on the street, sent a jolt of alarm through him. Sleep became a battleground; he would lie awake for hours, convinced that he had to stay alert, that some unforeseen danger was lurking just beyond his awareness. This pervasive sense of threat only made his mind more susceptible to the memories, creating a vicious feedback loop where the fear of the memory made the memory more likely to appear, and its appearance confirmed that the world was an unsafe place.

Over time, Arthur’s interpretation of the event and his reaction to it began to harden into a set of painful beliefs about himself. He was no longer just a man who had made a terrible mistake; he had come to believe he was fundamentally inadequate, a danger to the people he loved most. He saw his anxiety not as a normal reaction to trauma, but as proof that he was a lousy coper, weak and broken. These convictions poisoned his daily life. When he saw his grandson, the thought “I am a danger” would surface instantly, a judgment that felt as real and solid as the floor beneath his feet. This appraisal made the very sight of his family, once his greatest joy, a source of acute distress. The belief that he was permanently changed for the worse made him actively scan for evidence of his own incompetence, making him hypersensitive to triggers.

The maintaining cycles have now become deeply entrenched. His constant, humming state of hypervigilance means any unexpected stimulus feels like a threat, turning neutral events into triggers. At work, the stress of a long queue or an irritable customer is no longer just an annoyance; it’s a confirmation of his inability to cope. When Mary places a hand on his shoulder without warning, he flinches violently, the unexpected touch catapulting him back to the chaos of the accident. His recoil then fuels the appraisal that he is broken, that his reactions prove he is a bad coper. It is this conviction of his own inadequacy that seems to call forth the memories. Whenever he thinks, “I have ruined my family,” his mind dutifully supplies the evidence: the image of Leo on the concrete floor, the sound of the ambulance siren. The memory serves as proof for the negative appraisal, cementing it further.

He has started avoiding family dinners, making excuses that Mary knows are flimsy. The strain on their marriage is palpable. He hasn’t been in his garage since the accident and refuses to even change a lightbulb, abdicating all household tasks he once took pride in. It was after he refused to attend Leo’s sixth birthday party, terrified he might somehow cause another accident, that Mary insisted he seek help. Arthur agreed, not with hope, but with a quiet desperation. He feels he has permanently changed for the worse, but a small part of him still yearns for the day he can hug his grandson without the crushing weight of his own guilt and fear.
